You are an expert peer reviewer for Nature Communications, one of the world's leading multidisciplinary journals.

Read the following paper carefully and write a thorough, technically rigorous peer review. Identify the most important scientific concerns regarding: methodology, statistical analysis, data quality, claims vs. evidence, reproducibility, and clarity. Organise your review with clear sections.

## Abstract

Controlling complex light waves to achieve desired behaviours or characteristics on demand presents a significant challenge. This task becomes even more complicated when manipulating speckled light beams, owing to their inherently fuzzy intensity and phase structures. Here we demonstrate that a weak speckled second-harmonic signal in a multimode graded-index fibre can be manipulated via its conservative interaction with a high-power co-propagating fundamental pump wave. Specifically, the spatial quality of the signal can be either enhanced or degraded by varying the pump’s power or its modal distribution. The underlying physical mechanism is the optically induced mode conversion that can be controlled by the pump beam shape. This phenomenon enables new possibilities to manipulate complex light in nonlinear multimode waveguides. A striking example of this novel light-by-light control is the experimentally observed enhancement or partial suppression of the visible Raman Stokes cascade regulated by the second harmonic beam, while modulated by the mode power distribution of the fundamental beam.

---

## Introduction

The manipulation of light-by-light through cross-phase modulation (XPM) via the Kerr effect was extensively studied in the 1980s and 1990s [1-7]. The Kerr-induced cross-action of an intense pump light beam can alter a weak copropagating probe beam's temporal, spectral and spatial profiles. This interaction occurs conservatively without any power exchange between the pump and the probe. For instance, the additional phase shift that is induced by the strong wave may enable phase-matching between a fundamental frequency (FF) beam and its second harmonic (SH), allowing the control of nonlinear frequency conversion processes [8]. A lesser-known method for conservative control between light beams of different frequencies is the optically induced mode coupling (OIMC). This parametric interaction permits frequency translation without exponential gain, thereby avoiding spontaneous noise emission. As a result, the frequency translation associated with OIMC preserves the quantum state of a signal [9-10]. OIMC can involve two pumps at different wavelengths: maximum conversion efficiency from a signal to an idler is obtained at phase matching, under various configurations of polarization states, spatial modes, and wavelengths for pumps, signals, and idlers [9,12-13].

Nonlinear effects in multimode optical fibres provide a leap in our capacity for all-optical light manipulation: recent experiments have revealed that controlling the input wavefront permits to shape the spatial, temporal, and spectral properties of highly multimode beams [14-15]. In this framework, the effect of Kerr beam self-cleaning (BSC) [16-27], which allows the transformation of a speckle into a quasi-single-mode beam at the output of a graded-index (GRIN) highly multimode optical fibre (MMF), is particularly intriguing. BSC was initially interpreted as a nonlinear interaction between linear beam self-imaging and Kerr nonlinearity. The resulting nonlinear refractive index long-period grating [16-17] facilitates the phase-matching of frequency degenerate inter-modal four-wave mixing (IM-FWM), thus enhancing the nonlinear power redistribution [17-19]. From the application point of view, the most important aspect of BSC is the enhancement of the beam spatial quality, that is, the quenching of the beam’s M2 factor. Although it is a purely conservative process, BSC has also been observed in lossy and gain fibres [25-26] and in active tapers [28-29]. This has opened a new avenue for developing powerful fibre lasers operating in Q-switched or mode-locked configurations [26-27, 30-33]. Experiments have shown that BSC maintains the spatial coherence of the input laser [34], which enables new applications, such as imaging through MMFs [35].

Nevertheless, explaining the underlying mechanism for BSC has led to an ongoing controversial debate. Currently, the most widely accepted theory of BSC is based on thermodynamic considerations [36-38]. Within such a theoretical framework, the concept of BSC has been extended to the nonlinear dynamics of two co-propagating, orthogonally polarized beams [39-42]. However, experimental demonstrations of BSC involving multiple beams have so far been limited to a single strong carrier wavelength, thus preventing applications of this effect to polychromatic beams. Our approach opens new opportunities for supercontinuum generation in multimode fibers by exploiting the spatial overlap between high- and low-power multicolor beams. New perspectives also include the improved spatial quality control of multimode laser sources, and the possibility of ultrafast routing and switching between different channels in the telecommunications domain.

In this work, we elevate the field of light manipulation in MMFs to a new dimension, involving the nonlinear interaction among multiple laser beams of different carrier wavelengths. We experimentally demonstrate that the evolution of a weak speckled beam in the visible range can be controlled using a combination of XPM and nondegenerate OIMC with an intense pump beam in the near infrared, which undergoes its own spatial reshaping through the Kerr BSC process, but also its own spectral broadening by means of the Raman scattering process and soliton generation dynamics for very high peak powers. In our experiments the FF infrared beam at 1030 nm is provided by a Yb laser, while the visible beam is obtained via a nonlinear conversion from FF to SH (515 nm). Both beams are simultaneously injected into a GRIN MMF. By varying the power and modal distribution of the FF beam, the M² quality factor of the visible SH beam at the MMF output can be either decreased (beam cross-cleaning, BXC) or increased (beam cross-spoiling, BXS). The associated modification of the mode power distribution of the SH beam results from phase-matched IM-FWM-induced energy exchanges between its guided modes, driven by the intense FF beam. This mechanism for controlling the power exchange between modes can be compared, by analogy, to an intra-fiber controllable active spatial diffuser, sending energy from mode to mode on demand. In a first series of experiments using short laser pulses, the effect is limited by dispersive temporal walk-off. In a second set of experiments, employing long laser pulses in stead, we show that beam cross-interactions can significantly alter the beam shape of Raman cascade of Stokes lines. In this case, our experiments reveal that it is possible to reshape the number and modal content of the Stokes lines generated by a visible light beam by controlling the spatial profile and power of the near-infrared beam. We corroborate our observations through numerical simulations. Additional elements can be found in the supplementary material. Nonlinear shaping of the spatial profile of a laser beam using another laser beam paves the way for applications such as beam switching or manipulation in ultrafast regimes, e.g., for deep biological imaging.

---

## Results

Experimental results. In our experiments (Figure 1(a)), a Gaussian beam composed of 100 ps chirped pulses at 1030 nm is first split into its two orthogonal polarization components with adjustable powers (Figure 1(a)). The vertical component of the fundamental frequency (FF) pump beam is converted to its second harmonic (SH) by a type I BBO crystal positioned for strong phase mismatch conditions; the unconverted portion of the FF is filtered out. Next, the SH is temporally and spatially superimposed with the horizontal component of the FF beam by a beam splitter and a half-waveplate, before being coupled into the 50/125 µm GRIN fibre (see supplementary section 7). Under these conditions, both beams retain horizontal linear polarization, and their coupling efficiencies into the fibre can be adjusted. The green beam at 515 nm is weak enough, so that its own propagation in the fibre is purely linear. On the other hand, the pump beam may undergo spatial BSC thanks to its high peak power (see supplementary section 2). As a result, the transverse intensity profile of the pump beam at the fibre output evolves into a clean bell shape, which is observable in both near and far fields. By adjusting the delay line between the visible SH weak beam and the strong FF pump, so that the corresponding pulses no longer overlap in time, we verified that the weak SH beam remained unchanged, even in the presence of the FF beam. Conversely, when pulse synchronization among FF and SH pulses is well-tuned, we observed significant changes in the spatial distribution of the SH at 515 nm. These could be controlled by varying the power of the FF pump beam at 1030 nm, or its spatial coupling conditions. To further investigate this process, we analysed the near (Figures 1(c) and 1(d)) and far fields of the weak SH beam and performed numerical processing of both fields. This allowed the calculation of the beams’ spatial phase and M² coefficients, helping to identify their modal energy distribution (Figures 1(b,e,f), respectively).

For the first setting of the input coupling conditions of the FF beam into the fibre (i.e., straight on axis), we observed that increasing the FF power led to mode power redistribution for the SH, whereby lower-order modes (LOMs) of the SH are favoured with respect to higher-order modes (HOMs). This spatial beam reshaping, or BXC, is obtained by the OIMC process, which does not lead to energy exchange between the FF and the SH beams. Our analysis of near and far-field images at the fibre output confirms the beam cross-shaping. The M² coefficient of the SH beam, calculated by standard definitions [43], followed the same trend, decreasing along both the X and Y directions as the FF power grew larger (Figure 1(b), right). The maximum FF peak power in our experiment was approximately 40 kW, limited by input face fibre degradation. This power value remains far below levels typically associated with self-focusing effects.

We could reverse the beam interaction dynamics by slightly adjusting the FF beam’s input conditions (i.e., its focus point). Increasing the FF peak power led to a mode power redistribution for the SH, favouring HOMs. This BXS of the SH beam was accompanied by a corresponding increase of its M² coefficient (Figure 1(b), left). Near and far-field analyses confirmed this opposite trend. As we shall see in the subsequent theory section, the redistribution of energy between LOMs and HOMs of the SH beam is driven by the mode power distribution of the pump beam. That is, the FF beam modifies via OIMC the mode content of the weak SH beam. This may change the direction of energy flow among the modes of the SH beam, as testified by the corresponding decrease or increase of its quality factor. The occurrence of BXC or BXS in the SH beam is governed by nonlinear phase shifts, which either preserve or break phase-matching in the OIMC process, respectively.

In a second series of experiments (Figure 2), we excited additional modes in the FF to achieve a better spatial overlap with the SH. In this scenario, BSC efficiency for the FF beam was reduced, a bell-shaped beam is no longer formed at the fibre output (Figure 2 (a)). Nevertheless, by increasing the FF power we observed a gradual increase in the fundamental mode population of the SH beam (see Figure 2(b) and 2(c)). Maximum SH BXC was observed for input FF peak powers close to 23 kW, leading to a corresponding reduction of the M² coefficient for the SH beam. However, the process reversed at higher input FF powers (up to 100 kW), even without altering the input coupling conditions. Namely, the proportion of energy in the fundamental and other LOMs of the SH beam now decreases as the FF power grows larger (Figure 2(b)). In this regime, HOMs of the SH beam get progressively more populated, which can be interpreted as BXS, leading to an increased SH beam divergence at the fibre output. It is important to note that, to increase the peak power up to 100 kW, it was necessary to reduce the pulse duration from 100 ps down to 10 ps in order to avoid fibre damaging. This was achieved using the same initial 250 fs Fourier transform limited pump beam (see Methods) and changing the stretching passing from 100 ps to 10 ps.

As we have seen, the BXC efficiency can be limited either by the input FF peak power or by the temporal walk-off between FF and SH pulses. To further investigate the impact of BXC on multimode propagation, we conducted a third series of experiments where both individual SH and FF beams propagate in the fully nonlinear regime. We used a longer GRIN fibre (50 m) with a smaller core diameter (27 µm) (see also supplementary section 7); to minimize walk-off between the FF and the SH, we used another laser source that emits longer pulses, with a duration of 650 ps. By increasing the power of both SH and FF beams, while maintaining a peak power imbalance of 12:1 in favour of the infrared pump, we observed stimulated Raman scattering (SRS) cascades at both wavelengths, involving the generation of multiple Stokes lines (see Figure 3). The FF beam broadened spectrally beyond 1.3 µm, owing to Raman-shifted temporal soliton dynamics. On the other hand, SH propagation only produced Raman Stokes lines, because of the normal dispersion regime at the SH. Furthermore, both beams undergo nonlinear propagation leading to a spatial self-cleaning process and Raman beam clean-up, as already reported in the literature [18-20]. However, in the following paragraph, we present the impact of the cross-action between the two beams (FF+SH) on the SH beam, demonstrating BXC and BXS effects within the SH Raman cascade.

Nondegenerate OIMC between FF and SH beams established a direct link between the visible and fundamental Raman cascades. This interaction allowed the visible Raman cascade to be either enhanced by the BXC (Figures 3(a) and 3(b)) or suppressed (Figures 3(c) and 3(d)) by the BXS effects, induced by the FF pump beam before its spectral broadening. Mutual beam interaction dynamics depends on the intensity, polarization, and input coupling conditions of the infrared FF beam. The observed nonlinear beam dynamics in the presence of the Kerr effect and SRS resembles the behaviour observed in the pure Kerr case. Now, BXC redistributes the energy among the transverse modes of the SH beam, which controls its Raman gain and the associated Stokes cascade. This allowed us to determine the mode content of the beam by separating its spectral components by means of a grating, as depicted in Figure 3(e). Interestingly, we observed that the oscillating transverse mode of the Raman cascade could change (Figures 3(f) and 3(g)) and that the number of Stokes lines could be decreased with a change in the transverse mode (Figures 3(h) and 3(i)). This light-by-light switching was observed across varying numbers of Stokes lines, demonstrating that spatial reshaping of the SH beam preceded the generation of its own Stokes lines. We also note that the modal cascade with the appearance of the LP02-like mode remains stable over all three Stokes lines, apparently blocking or stabilizing the Raman beam clean-up process (Figure 3(f) and 3(g)). We also measured that more than 80% of the energy contained in the three Stokes Raman lines oscillating in the fundamental mode is transferred into the LP02-like mode, clearly illustrating the highly energetic impact that this cross-process can introduce.

Numerical results. We conducted numerical simulations to analyse the spatial reshaping of the weak SH beam under BXC or BXS, influenced by the FF beam. We used two coupled equations, one for the FF and one for the SH beam, which interact via asymmetric OIMC and XPM, owing to their different wavelengths, powers, and temporal walk-off between their pulses (see Methods). We also included the linear random mode coupling terms. In the linear propagation regime, no evolution of the beams was observed; all excited modes retain their energy, and the M² coefficient remains constant for both beams (see Supplementary section 3a). Simulations show the presence of a spatial BSC process (Figure 4) in the pump beam whenever its power grows above a certain threshold value. As a result, the weak SH beam undergoes BXC, with spatial remodelling leading to power transfer into its fundamental mode at the expense of HOMs (Figure 4(f)). This BXC occurs without any energy exchange between the two beams: no second-order nonlinearity is included in the model. Moreover, when the input peak power of the FF beam is further increased, we observed that BXC starts to saturate, until it gradually reverses (Figure 5). In this regime, the LOMs of the SH beam are now depleted in favour of its HOMs (Figure 5(f)). This inversion of behaviour occurs without any modification of the spatial input coupling conditions of the FF or the SH beams, at variance with the experimental results that we illustrated in Figure 2. Here, the only parameter that varied in our simulations was the FF input peak power. It is important to note that the brightness improvement of the FF pump beam associated with BSC remains limited when compared with the brightness improvement of the weak SH beam under BXC.

We considered input Gaussian beams for both the FF and the SH, centred on the fibre axis in simulations. As a result, only even modes are excited (Figure 4(c)(h) and Figure 5(c)(h)). In the occurrence of both BXC and BXS of the weak SH beam, we observed that odd modes remain largely unpopulated; this phenomenon has also been highlighted in the simpler case of BSC, as noted in [44]. The authors identified that mode groups containing radially symmetric modes are more populated than odd modes, a natural consequence of injecting a radially symmetric coherent beam into the MMF. They also noted that nonlinear modal interactions have varying efficiencies, due to the significant differences in nonlinear overlap coefficients between modes, which significantly affect the rate of convergence toward a steady-state mode power distribution.

Temporal walk-off between the weak SH and the infrared FF beam plays a significant role in the mechanism of BXC or BXS. To evaluate this, we ran numerical simulations without temporal walk-off (see Supplementary section 3b). The results revealed a significant increase in modulation from the infrared to the green beam, along with a more pronounced change in the M² coefficient. Experimentally, temporal walk-off can be minimized by using two closely spaced wavelengths, or a longer pulse relative to the propagation time in the fibre, as realized in our third experiment in strong nonlinear propagation regime involving a remodelling of the Raman cascade.

---

## Methods

Experiments. The detailed experimental setup is presented in Figure 1(a). It consists of a femtosecond-picosecond laser source delivering pulses between 250 fs and 100 ps (1030 nm), and a laser source with a pulse duration of 650 ps. The initial beam is separated into two parts using a polarizer and a half-wave plate. The first beam is converted into a BBO crystal cut for SH generation, and the remaining part of the infrared pump is removed using a BG18 filter. Thus, the SH is not generated inside the optical fiber, but it is coupled into it after conversion in a BBO crystal. The second part of the pump beam is attenuated by a passive filter and resynchronized with the SH of the first beam by means of two delay lines placed on each arm of the Mach-Zehnder interferometer. The synchronization accuracy is estimated to be 0.2 ps based on the optimization of the third harmonic generation correlation between SH and FF beams. A wideband dichroic plate is used. The two beams are temporally and spatially superimposed at the fibre input with linear polarization states by using a half-wave plate at the FF wavelength placed before the coupling lens. The fibre excitation process is carried out using a converging lens with a focal length of 50 mm. The output beams are analysed by two CCD cameras, allowing near- and far-field recordings for both beams. The first fibre is a 10 m long GRIN 50/125 µm multimode guide. A second GRIN fibre, 50 m long with a 27 µm core diameter, is instead used for Raman cascade generation. The images on Figures 3(f), 3(g), 3(h) and 3(i) are obtained by spatio-spectral analysis, using an optical grating to disperse the light in the horizontal dimension and reveal the far-field image of the beam in the vertical plane (Figure 3(e)). The results presented in Figures 2 and 3 are obtained by observing the green beam in the near-field domain and by readjusting only the coupling of the FF beam. The far-field associated with the green beam is then obtained in a second step, when collecting the final results.

### Reviewer 1

The manuscript presents an approach utilizing optically induced mode coupling (OIMC) and cross-phase modulation (XPM) to realize spatial mode modulation between beams of different frequencies in multimode optical systems. The experimental results demonstrate two key effects: (i) In the absence of energy exchange, a strong fundamental frequency (FF) pump beam can bidirectionally modulate the spatial mode distribution of a weak second harmonic (SH) beam, leading to either beam cross-conversion (BXC), characterized by low-order mode enhancement, or beam cross-switching (BXS), characterized by high-order mode enhancement; (ii) This modulation mechanism significantly impacts the SH beam’s mode composition, beam quality, and nonlinear Raman cascade behavior.
Additionally, numerical simulations validate the influence of FF power on the SH mode distribution and highlight the crucial role of temporal walk-off in the modulation process. The simulated results seem to be in good agreement with experimental observations.
Overall, the work provides a different perspective on optical control in multimode systems. However, I am unable to recommend the manuscript for publication in its current form. Below, I outline several questions and suggestions for the authors to address:
General comments:
As is well known, standard multimode fibers (MMFs), such as silica-based graded-index (GRIN) fibers, do not exhibit second-order nonlinear effects like second harmonic generation (SHG) under normal conditions due to the centrosymmetric nature of the material, which prohibits second-order susceptibility (χ(2)). Therefore, it is unclear how the authors achieve SHG, Raman Stokes cascades, and cross-phase modulation (XPM) via the Kerr effect simultaneously within the same GRIN MMF. The manuscript should clearly explain the physical mechanisms and nonlinear processes involved, especially how SHG is realized in such a system. If SHG occurs through special means—such as surface-induced symmetry breaking, quasi-phase matching, or use of non-silica dopants—those conditions and techniques must be explicitly detailed and justified.
As the authors are aware, beam self-cleaning (BSC) in multimode fibers is a well-established nonlinear phenomenon that has been extensively studied in the literature. It is generally understood within the framework of four-wave mixing (FWM), nonlinear mode coupling, and optical thermalization processes. In light of this, the manuscript should clarify how the proposed XPM-induced BSC fits within or deviates from this established theoretical framework. Specifically, the authors should elaborate on whether the observed effects are a novel manifestation of existing BSC mechanisms or represent a fundamentally new regime. A more rigorous theoretical discussion, possibly comparing the dynamics and physical conditions of XPM-induced BSC with traditional FWM- and thermalization-driven models, would be necessary and valuable for positioning this work within the broader context of nonlinear multimode optics.
Other comments and suggestions:
1. On the Energy Exchange Between FF and SH Beams: The authors should provide a more detailed evaluation, either experimental or theoretical, to confirm whether there is indeed no significant power exchange between the fundamental frequency (FF) and second harmonic (SH) beams. In high-power nonlinear regimes, energy transfer can critically affect the modal power balance of the SH beam, and this needs to be rigorously ruled out to support the core assumption of purely optically induced mode coupling (OIMC).
2. On the Nature of the Mode Power Distribution in Figure 2(c): The power distribution of the SH modes shown in Figure 2(c) appears unusually smooth, which raises the question of whether it represents a single-shot measurement or an averaged statistical result. In practice, such idealized mode profiles are rarely observed, especially under strong nonlinear propagation. The authors are encouraged to clarify the data processing method and compare it to more realistic cases, such as Figure S5 in Nature Physics 2022, 18, 685–690, where fluctuations in power distribution are evident.
3. On the Counterintuitive Modal Inversion at High FF Power: The authors report a reversal of modal energy flow at FF peak powers approaching 100 kW, where high-order modes (HOMs) of the SH beam become increasingly populated. This behavior is counterintuitive and requires further explanation. Specifically, the authors should assess whether the FF power in a 10 m fiber segment exceeds the thresholds for stimulated Raman scattering (SRS) or soliton formation. If such nonlinear effects are present, the observed behavior cannot be solely attributed to OIMC and may involve more complex nonlinear dynamics.
4. On the Impact of Pulse Duration Compression: To achieve 100 kW peak power, the pulse duration was reduced from 100 ps to 10 ps, which implies a significant increase in spectral bandwidth due to the time-bandwidth product. The authors should clarify whether this spectral broadening introduces any additional dispersion or nonlinear effects that might influence OIMC or the Raman cascade dynamics. Such effects could affect the interpretation of mode control results.
5. On the Feasibility of Temporal Overlap Between FF and SH Pulses: Given the group velocity mismatch between FF and SH wavelengths, achieving precise temporal and spatial overlap of low-coherence pulses is highly non-trivial. The authors are encouraged to provide a detailed and quantitative assessment of how this synchronization is achieved in the experiment, including potential experimental uncertainties. Without such justification, the validity of the claimed nonlinear interactions between temporally synchronized FF and SH pulses may be called into question.6. In the introduction section where the research background and methodology are presented, the motivation is currently summarized in only one sentence: “However, to our knowledge, experimental demonstrations of BSC involving multiple beams have been limited to a single carrier wavelength.” It would improve the manuscript if the authors could elaborate more on the research objectives and significance to better frame the study purpose.
7. The clarity and presentation of the figures should be improved to enhance overall readability. In particular, important annotations or explanatory labels should be added to guide the reader. For example, in Figure 1, the two different mechanisms could be more clearly distinguished—either by explicitly labeling them or by using visual aids such as dividing lines, shading, or color coding. This would help readers better understand the conceptual differences and the structure of the figure at a glance.
8. The manuscript frequently refers to supplementary materials for key data and conclusions, such as in the last paragraph of the first section. It would enhance the flow and comprehensiveness of the paper if some of this supplementary information were integrated into the main text. Also, the referencing of supplementary materials should be organized more systematically and judiciously throughout the article.
9. Several statements in the manuscript are unclear and should be revised for better clarity. For example, in the key paragraph starting at line 65, the sentence “In our experiments, the visible green beam is the SH of a Yb laser, which is used as the FF infrared control beam” is confusing and needs clarification—particularly the identification of the control beam and the actual role of the fundamental frequency (FF) and second harmonic (SH) beams. Additionally, the phrase “This mechanism acts as an active diffuser…” is potentially misleading. In the context of speckled beams, a “diffuser” typically refers to a physical element (e.g., ground glass) that alters speckle size or spatial coherence. It would be helpful for the authors to clarify this analogy if any, or consider using a different phrase as it involves different physics.

### Reviewer 2

In this manuscript, the authors propose an approach to controlling the spatial quality of multi-mode fiber (MMF) guided light beams, through a light-by-light scheme. They simultaneously inject high-power fundamental frequency (FF) light and low-power second harmonic (SH) light into a graded-index (GRIN) MMF, and achieve spatial quality adjustment of the SH light by changing the power and modal power distribution of the FF light. Different from the light-by-light control in traditional optical switches, this manuscript explores the possibility of controlling the signal light using pump light at different wavelength. Two sets of experiments are carried out to demonstrate their concept: i) They co-propagate FF light and SH light in a 10 m 50/125 GRIN MMF, and then alter the intensity of FF light and characterize the output light fields to demonstrate their approach; ii) They choose a longer-pulse source and a 50 m MMF with a 27 µm core diameter to obtain stronger nonlinearity, leading to adjustment of the number and mode components of the Stokes lines.
In my opinion, the proposed approach even though interesting does not provide convincing and significant novelty or impact to guarantee its publication in such a high impact journal. Additional comments are listed below for the authors to take into account prior to resubmitting their manuscript to another journal.
1.My major concern is, results in Fig. 1 and Fig. 2 are too weak to convince me. For instance, for the beam-cross cleaning (BXC) process in Fig. 1 (b), there are no obvious changes of M2. These discrete results are more like measured results that fluctuate within a limited range. I also don't see obvious beam-cleaning or beam-spoiling effect from the Fig. 1 (c) and (d). Similarly, results in Fig. 2 are also too weak. The mode distribution of SH light has only changed slightly, and there is no obvious beam-cleaning phenomenon.
2.Furthermore, such a beam cleaning strength, which may only enable the M2 of SH beam optimize from 11 to 10, will greatly limit the application of the method in this manuscript. Since the spatial quality of beams with M2 greater than 10 is still very poor. Thus, I can’t judge that the proposed approach has significant impact.
3.For the results with stronger nonlinearity (Fig. 3), is it possible to accomplish BXC process? The authors say that ‘Additionally, for both beams nonlinear propagation leads to both spatial BSC and Raman beam clean-up, which concentrate the beam energy into their LOMs (not shown here).’ It is confusing. A superior beam-cleaning result (e.g., optimized intensity profile or M2, etc.) in this case may be more convincing.
4.Does the proposed approach only work for the same laser source? In this manuscript, the authors use the FF and SH beam of the same laser source to demonstrate their approach (for a better spatiotemporal overlap?). However, if one can spatial-split such a laser source into two parts (with the same wavelength), one part is able to clean-up the other part with high quality. Obviously, the process of spatial split may be simpler than using a BBO to obtain its SH beam. Thus, a demo that verifies another laser source (with wavelength different from the signal beam) can clean-up the signal beam may be more convincing, which may demonstrate the potentially broad application scenarios.

Title: Spatio-spectral light-by-light moulding in multimode fibre
Authors: Yago Arosa, et. al.
In the field of beam transmission, multimode optical fibers (MMFs) have become the preferred medium for delivering high-power structured laser beams, attributed to their superior power-handling capabilities and modal diversity. Notably, the nonlinear effects intrinsic to MMFs present novel opportunities for achieving all-optical control. Nevertheless, the manipulation of speckled beams with complex spatial distributions remains a significant considerable challenge due to the inherently fuzzy intensity and phase structures. Diverging from prior research that predominantly concentrated on single-wavelength nonlinear control, this manuscript offers an innovative exploration of the nonlinear interaction mechanisms of dual-wavelength beams within MMFs. This approach broadens the scope of optical manipulation in MMFs, introducing a new dimension of multi-wavelength cooperative control. The findings illustrate that nonlinear interactions between fundamental-wavelength beam and its harmonic can be effectively regulated via optically induced mode coupling (OIMC) and cross-phase modulation (XPM), and thereby enhancing better spatial beam quality. Furthermore, by adjusting the modal power distribution of the second-harmonic signal, the visible Raman-Stokes cascade can be either enhanced or partially suppressed, highlighting the potential of multi-wavelength nonlinear effects for all-optical control. ## Paper

## Abstract

Controlling complex light waves to achieve desired behaviours or characteristics on demand presents a significant challenge. This task becomes even more complicated when manipulating speckled light beams, owing to their inherently fuzzy intensity and phase structures. Here we demonstrate that a weak speckled second-harmonic signal in a multimode graded-index fibre can be manipulated via its conservative interaction with a high-power co-propagating fundamental pump wave. Specifically, the spatial quality of the signal can be either enhanced or degraded by varying the pump’s power or its modal distribution. The underlying physical mechanism is the optically induced mode conversion that can be controlled by the pump beam shape. This phenomenon enables new possibilities to manipulate complex light in nonlinear multimode waveguides. A striking example of this novel light-by-light control is the experimentally observed enhancement or partial suppression of the visible Raman Stokes cascade regulated by the second harmonic beam, while modulated by the mode power distribution of the fundamental beam.

---

## Introduction

The manipulation of light-by-light through cross-phase modulation (XPM) via the Kerr effect was extensively studied in the 1980s and 1990s [1-7]. The Kerr-induced cross-action of an intense pump light beam can alter a weak copropagating probe beam's temporal, spectral and spatial profiles. This interaction occurs conservatively without any power exchange between the pump and the probe. For instance, the additional phase shift that is induced by the strong wave may enable phase-matching between a fundamental frequency (FF) beam and its second harmonic (SH), allowing the control of nonlinear frequency conversion processes [8]. A lesser-known method for conservative control between light beams of different frequencies is the optically induced mode coupling (OIMC). This parametric interaction permits frequency translation without exponential gain, thereby avoiding spontaneous noise emission. As a result, the frequency translation associated with OIMC preserves the quantum state of a signal [9-10]. OIMC can involve two pumps at different wavelengths: maximum conversion efficiency from a signal to an idler is obtained at phase matching, under various configurations of polarization states, spatial modes, and wavelengths for pumps, signals, and idlers [9,12-13].

Nonlinear effects in multimode optical fibres provide a leap in our capacity for all-optical light manipulation: recent experiments have revealed that controlling the input wavefront permits to shape the spatial, temporal, and spectral properties of highly multimode beams [14-15]. In this framework, the effect of Kerr beam self-cleaning (BSC) [16-27], which allows the transformation of a speckle into a quasi-single-mode beam at the output of a graded-index (GRIN) highly multimode optical fibre (MMF), is particularly intriguing. BSC was initially interpreted as a nonlinear interaction between linear beam self-imaging and Kerr nonlinearity. The resulting nonlinear refractive index long-period grating [16-17] facilitates the phase-matching of frequency degenerate inter-modal four-wave mixing (IM-FWM), thus enhancing the nonlinear power redistribution [17-19]. From the application point of view, the most important aspect of BSC is the enhancement of the beam spatial quality, that is, the quenching of the beam’s M2 factor. Although it is a purely conservative process, BSC has also been observed in lossy and gain fibres [25-26] and in active tapers [28-29]. This has opened a new avenue for developing powerful fibre lasers operating in Q-switched or mode-locked configurations [26-27, 30-33]. Experiments have shown that BSC maintains the spatial coherence of the input laser [34], which enables new applications, such as imaging through MMFs [35].

Nevertheless, explaining the underlying mechanism for BSC has led to an ongoing controversial debate. Currently, the most widely accepted theory of BSC is based on thermodynamic considerations [36-38]. Within such a theoretical framework, the concept of BSC has been extended to the nonlinear dynamics of two co-propagating, orthogonally polarized beams [39-42]. However, experimental demonstrations of BSC involving multiple beams have so far been limited to a single strong carrier wavelength, thus preventing applications of this effect to polychromatic beams. Our approach opens new opportunities for supercontinuum generation in multimode fibers by exploiting the spatial overlap between high- and low-power multicolor beams. New perspectives also include the improved spatial quality control of multimode laser sources, and the possibility of ultrafast routing and switching between different channels in the telecommunications domain.

In this work, we elevate the field of light manipulation in MMFs to a new dimension, involving the nonlinear interaction among multiple laser beams of different carrier wavelengths. We experimentally demonstrate that the evolution of a weak speckled beam in the visible range can be controlled using a combination of XPM and nondegenerate OIMC with an intense pump beam in the near infrared, which undergoes its own spatial reshaping through the Kerr BSC process, but also its own spectral broadening by means of the Raman scattering process and soliton generation dynamics for very high peak powers. In our experiments the FF infrared beam at 1030 nm is provided by a Yb laser, while the visible beam is obtained via a nonlinear conversion from FF to SH (515 nm). Both beams are simultaneously injected into a GRIN MMF. By varying the power and modal distribution of the FF beam, the M² quality factor of the visible SH beam at the MMF output can be either decreased (beam cross-cleaning, BXC) or increased (beam cross-spoiling, BXS). The associated modification of the mode power distribution of the SH beam results from phase-matched IM-FWM-induced energy exchanges between its guided modes, driven by the intense FF beam. This mechanism for controlling the power exchange between modes can be compared, by analogy, to an intra-fiber controllable active spatial diffuser, sending energy from mode to mode on demand. In a first series of experiments using short laser pulses, the effect is limited by dispersive temporal walk-off. In a second set of experiments, employing long laser pulses in stead, we show that beam cross-interactions can significantly alter the beam shape of Raman cascade of Stokes lines. In this case, our experiments reveal that it is possible to reshape the number and modal content of the Stokes lines generated by a visible light beam by controlling the spatial profile and power of the near-infrared beam. We corroborate our observations through numerical simulations. Additional elements can be found in the supplementary material. Nonlinear shaping of the spatial profile of a laser beam using another laser beam paves the way for applications such as beam switching or manipulation in ultrafast regimes, e.g., for deep biological imaging.

---

## Results

Experimental results. In our experiments (Figure 1(a)), a Gaussian beam composed of 100 ps chirped pulses at 1030 nm is first split into its two orthogonal polarization components with adjustable powers (Figure 1(a)). The vertical component of the fundamental frequency (FF) pump beam is converted to its second harmonic (SH) by a type I BBO crystal positioned for strong phase mismatch conditions; the unconverted portion of the FF is filtered out. Next, the SH is temporally and spatially superimposed with the horizontal component of the FF beam by a beam splitter and a half-waveplate, before being coupled into the 50/125 µm GRIN fibre (see supplementary section 7). Under these conditions, both beams retain horizontal linear polarization, and their coupling efficiencies into the fibre can be adjusted. The green beam at 515 nm is weak enough, so that its own propagation in the fibre is purely linear. On the other hand, the pump beam may undergo spatial BSC thanks to its high peak power (see supplementary section 2). As a result, the transverse intensity profile of the pump beam at the fibre output evolves into a clean bell shape, which is observable in both near and far fields. By adjusting the delay line between the visible SH weak beam and the strong FF pump, so that the corresponding pulses no longer overlap in time, we verified that the weak SH beam remained unchanged, even in the presence of the FF beam. Conversely, when pulse synchronization among FF and SH pulses is well-tuned, we observed significant changes in the spatial distribution of the SH at 515 nm. These could be controlled by varying the power of the FF pump beam at 1030 nm, or its spatial coupling conditions. To further investigate this process, we analysed the near (Figures 1(c) and 1(d)) and far fields of the weak SH beam and performed numerical processing of both fields. This allowed the calculation of the beams’ spatial phase and M² coefficients, helping to identify their modal energy distribution (Figures 1(b,e,f), respectively).

For the first setting of the input coupling conditions of the FF beam into the fibre (i.e., straight on axis), we observed that increasing the FF power led to mode power redistribution for the SH, whereby lower-order modes (LOMs) of the SH are favoured with respect to higher-order modes (HOMs). This spatial beam reshaping, or BXC, is obtained by the OIMC process, which does not lead to energy exchange between the FF and the SH beams. Our analysis of near and far-field images at the fibre output confirms the beam cross-shaping. The M² coefficient of the SH beam, calculated by standard definitions [43], followed the same trend, decreasing along both the X and Y directions as the FF power grew larger (Figure 1(b), right). The maximum FF peak power in our experiment was approximately 40 kW, limited by input face fibre degradation. This power value remains far below levels typically associated with self-focusing effects.

We could reverse the beam interaction dynamics by slightly adjusting the FF beam’s input conditions (i.e., its focus point). Increasing the FF peak power led to a mode power redistribution for the SH, favouring HOMs. This BXS of the SH beam was accompanied by a corresponding increase of its M² coefficient (Figure 1(b), left). Near and far-field analyses confirmed this opposite trend. As we shall see in the subsequent theory section, the redistribution of energy between LOMs and HOMs of the SH beam is driven by the mode power distribution of the pump beam. That is, the FF beam modifies via OIMC the mode content of the weak SH beam. This may change the direction of energy flow among the modes of the SH beam, as testified by the corresponding decrease or increase of its quality factor. The occurrence of BXC or BXS in the SH beam is governed by nonlinear phase shifts, which either preserve or break phase-matching in the OIMC process, respectively.

In a second series of experiments (Figure 2), we excited additional modes in the FF to achieve a better spatial overlap with the SH. In this scenario, BSC efficiency for the FF beam was reduced, a bell-shaped beam is no longer formed at the fibre output (Figure 2 (a)). Nevertheless, by increasing the FF power we observed a gradual increase in the fundamental mode population of the SH beam (see Figure 2(b) and 2(c)). Maximum SH BXC was observed for input FF peak powers close to 23 kW, leading to a corresponding reduction of the M² coefficient for the SH beam. However, the process reversed at higher input FF powers (up to 100 kW), even without altering the input coupling conditions. Namely, the proportion of energy in the fundamental and other LOMs of the SH beam now decreases as the FF power grows larger (Figure 2(b)). In this regime, HOMs of the SH beam get progressively more populated, which can be interpreted as BXS, leading to an increased SH beam divergence at the fibre output. It is important to note that, to increase the peak power up to 100 kW, it was necessary to reduce the pulse duration from 100 ps down to 10 ps in order to avoid fibre damaging. This was achieved using the same initial 250 fs Fourier transform limited pump beam (see Methods) and changing the stretching passing from 100 ps to 10 ps.

As we have seen, the BXC efficiency can be limited either by the input FF peak power or by the temporal walk-off between FF and SH pulses. To further investigate the impact of BXC on multimode propagation, we conducted a third series of experiments where both individual SH and FF beams propagate in the fully nonlinear regime. We used a longer GRIN fibre (50 m) with a smaller core diameter (27 µm) (see also supplementary section 7); to minimize walk-off between the FF and the SH, we used another laser source that emits longer pulses, with a duration of 650 ps. By increasing the power of both SH and FF beams, while maintaining a peak power imbalance of 12:1 in favour of the infrared pump, we observed stimulated Raman scattering (SRS) cascades at both wavelengths, involving the generation of multiple Stokes lines (see Figure 3). The FF beam broadened spectrally beyond 1.3 µm, owing to Raman-shifted temporal soliton dynamics. On the other hand, SH propagation only produced Raman Stokes lines, because of the normal dispersion regime at the SH. Furthermore, both beams undergo nonlinear propagation leading to a spatial self-cleaning process and Raman beam clean-up, as already reported in the literature [18-20]. However, in the following paragraph, we present the impact of the cross-action between the two beams (FF+SH) on the SH beam, demonstrating BXC and BXS effects within the SH Raman cascade.

Nondegenerate OIMC between FF and SH beams established a direct link between the visible and fundamental Raman cascades. This interaction allowed the visible Raman cascade to be either enhanced by the BXC (Figures 3(a) and 3(b)) or suppressed (Figures 3(c) and 3(d)) by the BXS effects, induced by the FF pump beam before its spectral broadening. Mutual beam interaction dynamics depends on the intensity, polarization, and input coupling conditions of the infrared FF beam. The observed nonlinear beam dynamics in the presence of the Kerr effect and SRS resembles the behaviour observed in the pure Kerr case. Now, BXC redistributes the energy among the transverse modes of the SH beam, which controls its Raman gain and the associated Stokes cascade. This allowed us to determine the mode content of the beam by separating its spectral components by means of a grating, as depicted in Figure 3(e). Interestingly, we observed that the oscillating transverse mode of the Raman cascade could change (Figures 3(f) and 3(g)) and that the number of Stokes lines could be decreased with a change in the transverse mode (Figures 3(h) and 3(i)). This light-by-light switching was observed across varying numbers of Stokes lines, demonstrating that spatial reshaping of the SH beam preceded the generation of its own Stokes lines. We also note that the modal cascade with the appearance of the LP02-like mode remains stable over all three Stokes lines, apparently blocking or stabilizing the Raman beam clean-up process (Figure 3(f) and 3(g)). We also measured that more than 80% of the energy contained in the three Stokes Raman lines oscillating in the fundamental mode is transferred into the LP02-like mode, clearly illustrating the highly energetic impact that this cross-process can introduce.

Numerical results. We conducted numerical simulations to analyse the spatial reshaping of the weak SH beam under BXC or BXS, influenced by the FF beam. We used two coupled equations, one for the FF and one for the SH beam, which interact via asymmetric OIMC and XPM, owing to their different wavelengths, powers, and temporal walk-off between their pulses (see Methods). We also included the linear random mode coupling terms. In the linear propagation regime, no evolution of the beams was observed; all excited modes retain their energy, and the M² coefficient remains constant for both beams (see Supplementary section 3a). Simulations show the presence of a spatial BSC process (Figure 4) in the pump beam whenever its power grows above a certain threshold value. As a result, the weak SH beam undergoes BXC, with spatial remodelling leading to power transfer into its fundamental mode at the expense of HOMs (Figure 4(f)). This BXC occurs without any energy exchange between the two beams: no second-order nonlinearity is included in the model. Moreover, when the input peak power of the FF beam is further increased, we observed that BXC starts to saturate, until it gradually reverses (Figure 5). In this regime, the LOMs of the SH beam are now depleted in favour of its HOMs (Figure 5(f)). This inversion of behaviour occurs without any modification of the spatial input coupling conditions of the FF or the SH beams, at variance with the experimental results that we illustrated in Figure 2. Here, the only parameter that varied in our simulations was the FF input peak power. It is important to note that the brightness improvement of the FF pump beam associated with BSC remains limited when compared with the brightness improvement of the weak SH beam under BXC.

We considered input Gaussian beams for both the FF and the SH, centred on the fibre axis in simulations. As a result, only even modes are excited (Figure 4(c)(h) and Figure 5(c)(h)). In the occurrence of both BXC and BXS of the weak SH beam, we observed that odd modes remain largely unpopulated; this phenomenon has also been highlighted in the simpler case of BSC, as noted in [44]. The authors identified that mode groups containing radially symmetric modes are more populated than odd modes, a natural consequence of injecting a radially symmetric coherent beam into the MMF. They also noted that nonlinear modal interactions have varying efficiencies, due to the significant differences in nonlinear overlap coefficients between modes, which significantly affect the rate of convergence toward a steady-state mode power distribution.

Temporal walk-off between the weak SH and the infrared FF beam plays a significant role in the mechanism of BXC or BXS. To evaluate this, we ran numerical simulations without temporal walk-off (see Supplementary section 3b). The results revealed a significant increase in modulation from the infrared to the green beam, along with a more pronounced change in the M² coefficient. Experimentally, temporal walk-off can be minimized by using two closely spaced wavelengths, or a longer pulse relative to the propagation time in the fibre, as realized in our third experiment in strong nonlinear propagation regime involving a remodelling of the Raman cascade.

---

## Methods

Experiments. The detailed experimental setup is presented in Figure 1(a). It consists of a femtosecond-picosecond laser source delivering pulses between 250 fs and 100 ps (1030 nm), and a laser source with a pulse duration of 650 ps. The initial beam is separated into two parts using a polarizer and a half-wave plate. The first beam is converted into a BBO crystal cut for SH generation, and the remaining part of the infrared pump is removed using a BG18 filter. Thus, the SH is not generated inside the optical fiber, but it is coupled into it after conversion in a BBO crystal. The second part of the pump beam is attenuated by a passive filter and resynchronized with the SH of the first beam by means of two delay lines placed on each arm of the Mach-Zehnder interferometer. The synchronization accuracy is estimated to be 0.2 ps based on the optimization of the third harmonic generation correlation between SH and FF beams. A wideband dichroic plate is used. The two beams are temporally and spatially superimposed at the fibre input with linear polarization states by using a half-wave plate at the FF wavelength placed before the coupling lens. The fibre excitation process is carried out using a converging lens with a focal length of 50 mm. The output beams are analysed by two CCD cameras, allowing near- and far-field recordings for both beams. The first fibre is a 10 m long GRIN 50/125 µm multimode guide. A second GRIN fibre, 50 m long with a 27 µm core diameter, is instead used for Raman cascade generation. The images on Figures 3(f), 3(g), 3(h) and 3(i) are obtained by spatio-spectral analysis, using an optical grating to disperse the light in the horizontal dimension and reveal the far-field image of the beam in the vertical plane (Figure 3(e)). The results presented in Figures 2 and 3 are obtained by observing the green beam in the near-field domain and by readjusting only the coupling of the FF beam. The far-field associated with the green beam is then obtained in a second step, when collecting the final results.

## Your Original Review (Round 1)

### Reviewer 1

The manuscript presents an approach utilizing optically induced mode coupling (OIMC) and cross-phase modulation (XPM) to realize spatial mode modulation between beams of different frequencies in multimode optical systems. The experimental results demonstrate two key effects: (i) In the absence of energy exchange, a strong fundamental frequency (FF) pump beam can bidirectionally modulate the spatial mode distribution of a weak second harmonic (SH) beam, leading to either beam cross-conversion (BXC), characterized by low-order mode enhancement, or beam cross-switching (BXS), characterized by high-order mode enhancement; (ii) This modulation mechanism significantly impacts the SH beam’s mode composition, beam quality, and nonlinear Raman cascade behavior.
Additionally, numerical simulations validate the influence of FF power on the SH mode distribution and highlight the crucial role of temporal walk-off in the modulation process. The simulated results seem to be in good agreement with experimental observations.
Overall, the work provides a different perspective on optical control in multimode systems. However, I am unable to recommend the manuscript for publication in its current form. Below, I outline several questions and suggestions for the authors to address:
General comments:
As is well known, standard multimode fibers (MMFs), such as silica-based graded-index (GRIN) fibers, do not exhibit second-order nonlinear effects like second harmonic generation (SHG) under normal conditions due to the centrosymmetric nature of the material, which prohibits second-order susceptibility (χ(2)). Therefore, it is unclear how the authors achieve SHG, Raman Stokes cascades, and cross-phase modulation (XPM) via the Kerr effect simultaneously within the same GRIN MMF. The manuscript should clearly explain the physical mechanisms and nonlinear processes involved, especially how SHG is realized in such a system. If SHG occurs through special means—such as surface-induced symmetry breaking, quasi-phase matching, or use of non-silica dopants—those conditions and techniques must be explicitly detailed and justified.
As the authors are aware, beam self-cleaning (BSC) in multimode fibers is a well-established nonlinear phenomenon that has been extensively studied in the literature. It is generally understood within the framework of four-wave mixing (FWM), nonlinear mode coupling, and optical thermalization processes. In light of this, the manuscript should clarify how the proposed XPM-induced BSC fits within or deviates from this established theoretical framework. Specifically, the authors should elaborate on whether the observed effects are a novel manifestation of existing BSC mechanisms or represent a fundamentally new regime. A more rigorous theoretical discussion, possibly comparing the dynamics and physical conditions of XPM-induced BSC with traditional FWM- and thermalization-driven models, would be necessary and valuable for positioning this work within the broader context of nonlinear multimode optics.
Other comments and suggestions:
1. On the Energy Exchange Between FF and SH Beams: The authors should provide a more detailed evaluation, either experimental or theoretical, to confirm whether there is indeed no significant power exchange between the fundamental frequency (FF) and second harmonic (SH) beams. In high-power nonlinear regimes, energy transfer can critically affect the modal power balance of the SH beam, and this needs to be rigorously ruled out to support the core assumption of purely optically induced mode coupling (OIMC).
2. On the Nature of the Mode Power Distribution in Figure 2(c): The power distribution of the SH modes shown in Figure 2(c) appears unusually smooth, which raises the question of whether it represents a single-shot measurement or an averaged statistical result. In practice, such idealized mode profiles are rarely observed, especially under strong nonlinear propagation. The authors are encouraged to clarify the data processing method and compare it to more realistic cases, such as Figure S5 in Nature Physics 2022, 18, 685–690, where fluctuations in power distribution are evident.
3. On the Counterintuitive Modal Inversion at High FF Power: The authors report a reversal of modal energy flow at FF peak powers approaching 100 kW, where high-order modes (HOMs) of the SH beam become increasingly populated. This behavior is counterintuitive and requires further explanation. Specifically, the authors should assess whether the FF power in a 10 m fiber segment exceeds the thresholds for stimulated Raman scattering (SRS) or soliton formation. If such nonlinear effects are present, the observed behavior cannot be solely attributed to OIMC and may involve more complex nonlinear dynamics.
4. On the Impact of Pulse Duration Compression: To achieve 100 kW peak power, the pulse duration was reduced from 100 ps to 10 ps, which implies a significant increase in spectral bandwidth due to the time-bandwidth product. The authors should clarify whether this spectral broadening introduces any additional dispersion or nonlinear effects that might influence OIMC or the Raman cascade dynamics. Such effects could affect the interpretation of mode control results.
5. On the Feasibility of Temporal Overlap Between FF and SH Pulses: Given the group velocity mismatch between FF and SH wavelengths, achieving precise temporal and spatial overlap of low-coherence pulses is highly non-trivial. The authors are encouraged to provide a detailed and quantitative assessment of how this synchronization is achieved in the experiment, including potential experimental uncertainties. Without such justification, the validity of the claimed nonlinear interactions between temporally synchronized FF and SH pulses may be called into question.6. In the introduction section where the research background and methodology are presented, the motivation is currently summarized in only one sentence: “However, to our knowledge, experimental demonstrations of BSC involving multiple beams have been limited to a single carrier wavelength.” It would improve the manuscript if the authors could elaborate more on the research objectives and significance to better frame the study purpose.
7. The clarity and presentation of the figures should be improved to enhance overall readability. In particular, important annotations or explanatory labels should be added to guide the reader. For example, in Figure 1, the two different mechanisms could be more clearly distinguished—either by explicitly labeling them or by using visual aids such as dividing lines, shading, or color coding. This would help readers better understand the conceptual differences and the structure of the figure at a glance.
8. The manuscript frequently refers to supplementary materials for key data and conclusions, such as in the last paragraph of the first section. It would enhance the flow and comprehensiveness of the paper if some of this supplementary information were integrated into the main text. As is well known, standard multimode fibers (MMFs), such as silica-based graded-index
(GRIN) fibers, do not exhibit second-order nonlinear effects like second harmonic generation
(SHG) under normal conditions due to the centrosymmetric nature of the material, which
prohibits second-order susceptibility (χ(2)). Therefore, it is unclear how the authors achieve

Our Answer:
We agree with the Reviewer that SH generation is not possible in silica, and thus cannot occur

Reviewer 1 Comment:
As the authors are aware, beam self-cleaning (BSC) in multimode fibers is a well-established
nonlinear phenomenon that has been extensively studied in the literature. It is generally
understood within the framework of four-wave mixing (FWM), nonlinear mode coupling, and
optical thermalization processes. In light of this, the manuscript should clarify how the
proposed XPM-induced BSC fits within or deviates from this established theoretical
framework. Specifically, the authors should elaborate on whether the observed effects are a
novel manifestation of existing BSC mechanisms or represent a fundamentally new regime. A
more rigorous theoretical discussion, possibly comparing the dynamics and physical conditions
of XPM-induced BSC with traditional FWM- and thermalization-driven models, would be
necessary and valuable for positioning this work within the broader context of nonlinear
multimode optics.
Our Answer:
Indeed, the BSC arises from the coherent interaction between transverse modes in a multimode
fiber, and directly affects the power distribution among the modes. The combined effects of
linear (random) mode coupling, nonlinear Kerr process, and intermodal beating (self-imaging)
induce a periodic index grating that enables four-wave mixing and drives energy exchange
between modes. Under these conditions, the coupling strength is determined by self- and cross-
phase modulation between the modes of a single monochromatic coupled beam.
This interaction, governed by the initial power and its initial modal energy distribution, induces
a self-organized process that converges towards the limited number of stable states, most
notably the beam cleaning state.
In the present study, we replace the self-phase modulation with cross-phase modulation, which
can be introduced by an additional beam either coupled into or generated within the fiber core
at different initial wavelengths. While this does not change the principle of energy transfer
among modes, it significantly enhances its impact and enables new states to emerge at the fiber
output. Among them, the main and interesting effect is the ability to control the direction of
energy transfer between modes by means of a control beam, thereby modifying the dynamics
of energy propagation inside the fiber.
This new regime not only enables control of a weak beam at any different wavelength within
the fiber, but can also either improve or degrade its brightness. Furthermore, it allows one to
accelerate or slow down the intermodal energy transfer driven by random coupling. In this
work, the use of another copropagating beam at a different wavelength introduces additional
opportunities for achieving advanced control of light in multimode fibers.
As far as the comparison of our system and experimental results with “thermalization-driven
models”, in our Supplementary sections SI3 and SI4, we have presented numerical
computations of the entropy evolutions of the interacting fundamental and second-harmonic
beams. These intriguing results will certainly stimulate further theoretical studies for extending
current thermodynamic treatments to the case of multiple interacting beams. However, the
development of such theory is beyond the scope of our present work.
To follow the Reviewer's recommendation and to better illustrate the difference with the
standard BSC mechanism, we have added the following paragraph to the discussion section.
“The cross-beam interaction can be regarded as an extension of the BSC mechanism, in which
the self-phase modulation driving the cleaning process is replaced by a nonlinear phase shift
(or cross-phase modulation) induced through interaction with an additional beam. In other
words, the longitudinal grating formed in the BSC regime, arising from the combined action
of the Kerr effect and the self-imaging process in the parabolic fiber, can strongly impact other
beams, whether weak or strong, that propagate simultaneously within the fiber. This constitutes
a new nonlinear propagation regime that is more versatile and readily controllable.”

Additional comments are listed below for the authors to take into account prior to resubmitting
their manuscript to another journal.
Our Answer:
We are sorry about the unfavorable assessment of the novelty and impact of our paper by
Reviewer 2. However, we respectfully disagree with the Reviewer on this point: we firmly
believe that our study provides numerous new findings that will significantly contribute to the
science and technology of light-by-light control in optical fibers or fiber laser sources.
For instance, the key highlights of the novelty and impact of our paper include:
We have introduced and demonstrated experimentally and numerically the ability of complex
media such as multimode fibers to control the brightness of a weak or strong beam via its
interaction with an intense light of different wavelengths. This control can force spatial
focusing or defocusing, thanks to the manipulation of an energetic pump beam whose
propagation and coupling are fully controlled. Thus, this pump beam can act as an ultrafast
external optical control device, able to change the propagation dynamics and nonlinear
conversion of other beams. Our results will be extremely useful for many applications, such as
supercontinuum generation, where the pump beam can strongly influence the spatial and
spectral distribution of the converted wavelength, and also in the field of lasers, where the laser
wavelength could interact with the spatial distribution of the pump beam. Telecommunications
could also exploit such a modal connection to implement spatial switching for all-optical data
routing.
From a fundamental perspective, our results offer important insights for a thermodynamic
description of the light propagation, raising questions about cross-condensation phenomenon
previously observed and reported in other domains (see for example: the Claisen cross-
condensation - L. Claisen and A. Claparède, “Condensationen von Ketonen mit Aldehyden”,
Ber. Dtsch. Chem. Ges., vol. 14, no. 2, 1881, pp. 2460-2468, ISSN 0365-9496, DOI
10.1002/cber.188101402192, or the cross-aldolic-condensation in chemistry - L. G. Wade,
Organic Chemistry, Upper Saddle River (New Jersey), Prentice Hall, 2005 (6th ed.), ISBN
978-0-13-169957-1 and 0-13-169957-1, p. 1056-1066).
Another very interesting result, presented in this paper, is the cross-beam alteration of the low
intensity beam, which cannot be achieved through the spatial self-cleaning process. This
mechanism, which is essentially the inverse of the spatial self-cleaning process, expands our
ability to regulate the energy transfer to higher-order modes, thereby increasing the beam
expansion rate during propagation, that is, it can accelerate or slow down beam thermalization
in a multimode fiber. Consequently, the flow of beam entropy can be regulated by the power
of a copropagating beam. Beyond this demonstration, we also clearly show that the temporal
walk-off can significantly limit or enhance energy transfer, making it a key parameter to
consider. As a result, wavelengths close to or far from the pump wavelength can be affected
differently, introducing an additional interesting mechanism for spatial shaping in the
stimulated Raman process.
We have also demonstrated that a limited transformation effect at a given wavelength (e.g. the
SH of the pump wave) can drive the stimulated Raman effect from this SH wave to strongly
modify its spatial gain distribution and generate Stokes waves in a high-order mode in a stable
state. This was observed for the first three Stokes lines, which transferred nearly all the energy
from the fundamental mode to an LP02-like mode, thereby highlighting the high efficiency of
this spatial transformation. The almost total energy transfer achieved within the stimulated
Raman process represents a major novel and impactful result, showing the full potential of this
cross-modulation effect.
Moreover, we show, for the first time to our knowledge, that the Raman beam clean-up in
multimode fiber may be affected by copropagating beams, enabling the transformation of a
LP01 mode into a higher-order mode.
Finally, we have also numerically demonstrated that a low-intensity speckle beam can be
efficiently converted into a quasi-single mode by interaction with another pump beam speckle
at a different wavelength, achieving a total power transfer of more than 52% to the main mode
compared to 6% when cross-cleaning is not operating.
For all these reasons, we respectfully disagree with the Reviewer's opinion on the significance
of our work, thus precluding our manuscript from being considered for publication in Nature
Communication.

been published (see Journal of Lightwave Technology, 2023, 41, 3164) (Reference 40).
